newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Storm greets Renault plant closure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Storm greets Renault plant closure.

text.p: The decision by French car group Renault SA to shut its Vilvoorde plant near Brussels caused a storm of protest from Belgium and unions on Friday but it cheered the stock market.

Investors welcomed news of what they saw as Renault getting to grips with its cost structure and boosted the shares 13 percent. That came on top of a five percent gain made on Thursday when the closure was announced.

Belgian officials and newspaper were shocked at the death sentence for the plant, however. Car workers at Vilvoorde, the home town of Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, blocked the factory and prevented finished cars from leaving.
Dehaene told a news conference that his government was "indignant and stupefied" by the decision, which he called unacceptable. He will meet French Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Monday.
The Prime Minister of Flanders, the Dutch speaking part of Belgium that includes Vilvoorde, summoned Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer for a meeting in Brussels on Saturday.

The French Communist-led CGT union, outraged by the decision and fearing similar moves in France, called for "social disobediance" among its Renault members and joined other French unions in calling for a national day of protest on March 20.
"The only thing that counts is the wish of the financial world and of 'God CAC-40'," the CGT said in a statement referring to France's CAC-40 blue-chip share index.
The Force Ouvriere union said it expected more bad news shortly and feared another 3,000 jobs could be lost in 1997 among the 78,000 car workers at Renault plants in France.

French Labour Minister Jacques Barrot told French radio "the closure of (the plant in) Belgium is not a closure against Belgium. It is a technical closure because this plant made several models at the time and was not functional."
The European Commission said on Friday that Renault was obliged to go through the correct procedure before closing its Belgian plant.

Barbara Nolan, spokeswoman for social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn told Reuters that it was down to workers, trade unions or the Belgian state to take action if they believed Renault was closing the Vilvoorde plant without due consultation.
The French government still has a 46 percent stake in Renault, which was partially privatised in two stages in 1994 and 1996. It used to be a bastion of labour union power.

The company is expecting a sharp loss for 1996 -- estimated by a leading French financial newspaper at more than four billion francs ($701 million) -- because of weak markets, high costs and despite the launch of car models such as the Megane.
On Wednesday, the French government turned down a request by Renault and rival carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen to pay the bulk of a massive early retirement scheme.

The two companies want to reduce the average age and size of their workforce, among the oldest in the European car industry, to survive competition which is expected to become even fiercer when the market opens fully to Japanese competition in 2000.
